implementation_notes: Modern C++ makes the ownership half of Whole-Part part of the type system: parts that live exactly as long as the whole are member subobjects, parts that are optional, polymorphic or added and removed at runtime are std::unique_ptr members, and the whole's implicit destructor destroys all of them in reverse order of declaration - no Whole/Part role classes are needed. std::unique_ptr is also what makes the pImpl idiom work, where the whole's single part is an incomplete type in the header. The classic POSA form (an explicit Whole class with part-management operations) is still justified when part creation is driven by runtime configuration or must be lazy, but even then the parts stay uniquely owned.
pitfalls: Copying a whole that owns raw pointers aliases the parts and double-deletes them: delete the copy operations or own parts by value/unique_ptr so the whole is move-only or deep-copying.
A shared_ptr back-reference from a part to its whole closes a cycle that never releases the whole - use weak_ptr (or a raw observing pointer) for the part-to-whole link.
Destruction is reverse declaration order: a part whose destructor reads another member must be declared after it, otherwise it runs against an already-destroyed sibling.

variants.name: Handle/Body with a shared counted representation (copy-on-write)
variants.implementation_notes: When whole values are copied often and building the parts is expensive, keep one shared representation (the body) behind a handle and let copies share it until someone mutates: the mutating operation checks the shared_ptr use count and detaches - copies the body - before writing. POSA1 documents exactly this family (Counted Body, Counted Pointer, Handle-Body) among its C++ known uses of Whole-Part: the semantics stay those of an exclusively owned aggregation while the representation is reference counted. The price is an indirection on every access and copy-on-write bugs that only appear under aliasing, so choose it when copying dominates the profile.
pitfalls: One mutator that forgets the detach check writes through to every copy: copy-on-write bugs surface as aliasing, not as a crash.
shared_ptr cycles: if the body holds a shared_ptr back to the handle or to a sibling part, nothing is ever released - back links must be weak_ptr or raw observing pointers.
A detach inside a hot loop copies the whole aggregation; amortise the mutation or prefer the exclusive variant.
